I feel bad writing a not recommended review for this game, as you can tell passion went into it and there's clearly talent on display too.  But that's how I felt by the end.

Basically, this game starts out pretty fun, with a good style and really good score.  I love spaghetti westerns, and the influence on this is obvious, with several name checks including to some that casual fans won't know (The Great Silence, for instance), musical influence is there too, I enjoyed all that.  The core gameplay feels fine, at first.  I really like the duck companion who retrieves your throwing knife and is always present - great concept and well-executed.  The bosses are pretty good, if simple.  The luck stuff is interesting.

But eventually, the enemies get really excessively spongy, the difficulty climbs, and it gets annoying and not fun any more.  Like, imagine if you were playing Contra and the regular guys that run at you took EIGHT individual bullet hits, and you had to reload every six shots on top of that.  Reloading is also cancelled by jumping or the dodge roll, which just feels awkward, you have to hit the reload button almost as much as the fire button.  You have a throwing knife, but it's as weak as a bullet, rendering it almost pointless.  It all just kills the flow, you feel like you're cheesing the game just to kill standard enemies, running away to reload as they charge at you.

I also kept basically forgetting about luck.  It's there, I'd use it in tough sections, but it doesn't feel that well integrated with everything else.  

I really feel like they could have tweaked these different ingredients and made a better game out of them with much better combat flow.  How about if you're completely empty AND throw the knife, a dodge roll gives an auto reload?  How about rolling doesn't stop reloading?  Headshots do quadruple damage?  I don't know, something.  

There's also a couple other annoyances.  You can't completely skip boss cut scenes, so if you die it gets annoying.  You can also die AFTER a boss fight, and have to re-fight them.  

But, the core problem is just the combat gets tedious and the enemies stop being fun.  

I'll note - I did finish the game in about 2 hours with little serious difficulty, for those curious about the length.  Just the challenge wasn't a fun one - it was tedious.

I tried to like this game because I love both the Western genre and retro gaming. But this is just too broken.

- Can't skip cutscenes. Don't force players to watch the same junk over and over. It's salt in the wound, given the game's annoying difficulty.

- The difficulty is lazy. This seems to be the current rage in indie games. It's easier and cheaper to make a small game, and fill it with cheap deaths requiring numerous replays to simply take up time than it is to make a longer game with more thoughtful challenges. This is probably why you're forced to watch the same cutscenes and dialog over and over. (Spamming the action button to speed up repeat dialog doesn't help much.)

- The mechanism for reloading your gun is broken. Half the time the character only reloads half the cylinders. You have to spam the reload button just to reload 6 bullets, all while dodging excessive junk on the screen. Not cool.

- I get that it would be too easy if the enemies died after one or two shots. But having to shoot basic enemies 8 times (with a broken reload mechanism) is lousy.

- The 'luck' mechanism is mostly random, and mostly just distracting and annoying. You and/or your enemy will randomly avoid damage for a second. Tedious, especially against the overpowered bosses. (You can trigger it manually but not many times.)

- The bosses are overpowered. You only have to get hit 3 or 4 times and you're dead. The bosses? Their life bar is 20+ hits until they're dead. (Again, it's easier to make a short, cheaply hard game than a longer more thoughtful game.)

- This game runs rather poorly given it's ultra low fidelity. (This one I could overlook if it weren't for the above glaring flaws.) For example, why am I seeing a loading screen at all? I have it installed on a SSD with a 3080 ti GPU. This game already has enough repetitive junk, I don't want to wait for loading on a graphically simple game like this on higher-end hardware. (I'm assuming the occasional in-game stutters are pseudo, intentional nostalgia because my frame counter never drops. But if these aren't intentional, well...)

I wouldn't recommend this game at any price point, including free.

Sidescroll 'em up western with Commodore 64-esque graphics that allows you to store up luck to use as a resource and manipulate certain behind the scenes dicerolls to your favor (or against). Prevelant throughout is a minamalist hip-hop theme that mixes with the spaghetti western setting to create something extremely surreal - which is saying something for a title that also features a trusty duck companion who only acts [i]sort of[/i] like a mallard.

While the game begins charming and is an easy venture to get into the groove of (shoot, roll, jump and knifetoss to victory with the occasional item/luck medallion usage) certain gameplay flaws quickly become apparent. Reloading is an easily interrupted though setting appropriate juncture and there will be plenty of times where you'll be flanked on both sides stuck dodging while reloading one bullet at a time to peck away at enemies with. Throw in melee enemies that just run straight at you while the shooters are still there and you've got yourself the perfect formula for annoyance. Expect to meet such a gauntlet near the end of almost every level. On top of this is that getting hit and/or losing a life depletes your luck [spoiler]and I'm not sure if one of the last few jumps in the ice level is even possible if you've managed to find yourself without enough to luck to bounce out of the bottomless pit to clear it[/spoiler]

Bosses are a mixed bag of characters every last bit as crazy as the townfolk, my personal favorite being the saloon girl (incorporates a game of chance to determine how much of a disadvantage you start at) and the cultist priest being by far the most annoying (the battle IS the aforementioned gauntlet full of endless rushing melee enemies while having to dodge a fast giant coin). If you're unlucky enough to lose at a boss you don't get to start straight at the fight; you'll have to mash through the cutscene every single time. Not even the sick in-town skateboarding or freestyle instrumental recording you can do is enough to forgive such a thing in the modern day.

Had Luckslinger kept its initial impression it'd definitely be a thing to reccomend (though perhaps a stretch at that asking price), but it sadly ended up skipping a few too many beats and firing more blanks than lead for me. [spoiler]For whatever reason, the achievement for beating the game wasn't awarded either despite killing the sudden last boss and sitting through the credits, I'll chalk that up to an even more innovative creeping bad luck feature than I expected[/spoiler]

[spoiler]I haven't done a review for a game in a few years, so here's one on Luckslinger.[/spoiler]

[h1]Luckslinger is a game that doesn't seem to be popular in comparison to small indie games and even meme games, but it's a good game at best. Here are some things that I like, dislike, and neutral on Luckslinger but with a corny pun for what's listed.[/h1]

[b]The good:[/b]
+amazing soundtrack
+graphics are not flashy, but it's still designed well,
+The spaghetti western style is neat. It may not be 100% accurate, but I don't really care about that.
+The luck system is a nice concept done alright in the game. The entire premise on luck is essentially like this: the more luck you have, the less likely an unlucky event occurs and the more likely to get lucky events. You're also going to need to use your luck carefully and avoid getting hit/dying as that will decrease your luck to the point that it may be impossible to reach certain areas. If you're wanting to get all the goldbars during levels, you're going to need a lot of luck.
+The movement, shooting mechanics, dodging, and reloading are good.
+The price is fair. It's not expensive, but it was worth the cost in my opinion.

[b]The[/b] [i]not so[/i] [b]bad:[/b]
+/- The game is relatively short depending on how you do. My first playthough took me 7 hours until I just gave up and went for a second playthough about almost a year later. That second playthough went about around 5 and a half hours.
+/- The game requires A LOT of precision and concentration, especially when it comes to jumping from one platform to another. At times, I can be on a roll with a lot of dodging, and then there are times where I fail miserably.There were even times where I tried to jump on certain platforms only to completely miss and die.
+/- There are choices that you can make when it comes to defeating a boss, but whatever choice you choose has no effect on what happen on the game. The main changes that occur are mostly on how the jail cell and the graveyard looks.  [spoiler]The changes in the ending is only based on how much gold bars you have or if you talk to 1 of the 2 big fans in the town that appear after beating the second boss.[/spoiler] This game wasn't really designed for that purpose, so it's not that bad.
+/- All the characters aren't too memorable but are okay as they are. The most memorable character out of everyone is Duckbridge mainly for just [url=http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=876971452]blocking a cutscene randomly.[/url]
+/- The minigames are alright. However, most of the rewards given on each minigame are given once per level with the exception of poker since I only played it a few times and lost every time. Not to mention that the last time you do the shot chug minigame requires to press the button ridiculously fast. [spoiler]In fact, it was too fast for me to do with 1 controller, so if you're wanting that achievement to chug a large amount of shots in like 5 seconds, you're gonna need a gamepad and a keyboard to spam your way to the achievement.[/spoiler]

[b]The Ugly:[/b]
-If you're the kind of person that goes for 100% on achievements, this game may take you a long time, if not then never, to get as a couple of achievements are [i]literally[/i] questionable. [spoiler](apparently, they're based on actual chances and luck but not from the luck system itself)[/spoiler]
-Unskippable dialogue // I've died a lot of times on almost all the bosses, and there is no way to skip their dialogue, which gets irritating
-You cannot disable Auto Save as far as I know, which goes to my next negative.
-This is a bit of a nitpick, but I had went through a second runthrough attempting to get all the goldbars [spoiler]34/33 in total[/spoiler], and one of the ways to get a goldbar is by playing a certain pattern at Clovercreek's bank. Now, [spoiler]if you pause the game while inside the bank, Duckbridge will tell you the code with a questionmark.[/spoiler] You get 6 goldbars in total when you get the pattern right for all of them, but if you ♥♥♥♥ up, you won't be able to open it up until you beat the next level. During my run, I only got 4 out of the 6 [spoiler]even when I put on the code that Duckbridge gave.[/spoiler] What's worse is that since there's no auto save, I can't go back and try to redo it.

Luckslinger

Resumo:

Simples, divertido e carismático... Bom valor em produto: visual eficiente; mecânica simples, mas bem composta; excelente música; texto bem escrito e bem distribuído que consegue ser engraçado; difícil, mas bem variado e capaz de garantir 10 horas ou mais de genuína diversão, raiva e risadas.

Recomendo Luckslinger pelo preço total de R$ 19,99...
-50% durante promoções é um desconto mais que generoso...

-------------------------------------------
Então vamos, como de costume, para uma análise mais detalhada do jogo...

Luckslinger é um jogo de ação e plataforma que, mesmo em sua simplicidade, consegue ser super peculiar e cheio de identidade. Um jogo que chama o jogador para para confiar na sorte e sorrir da morte. Com um visual simples, mas cheio de cor e carisma e uma composição musical que faz muito mais que cobrir o fundo; uma trilha sonora boa o suficiente para valer a pena coletar ao longo das fases para escutar na tela inicial.

Mecanicamente, é um jogo difícil com uma boa variedade de inimigos e situações. Luckslinger conta com uma pistola, uma faca que ele pode lançar em seus inimigos, um pato sempre disposto a ajudar e, eventualmente, uma arma ou utilitário extra que pode ser coletado ao longo do caminho ou adquirido como prêmio em uma aposta.

Vá com calma, vá na manha... escute a música, estude as fases, tente dançar com cada cenário... caso contrário, você vai morrer... de novo e de novo e de novo... o jogo não é extremamente punitivo, fases salvam em checkpoints, mas podem parecer um tanto longas depois que você passa por metade delas mais de 3 vezes... uma vez que você percebe como cada fase e cada inimigo funciona, o jogo se torna muito mais divertido, ao ponto em que morrer pela 3a vez tentando algum truque diferente mais me faz rir que ter ódio... chefões são sempre diferentes e sempre capazes de fazer você sorrir e passar um pouco de raiva... adorável mistura...

Mas há também o fator sorte, daí o nome: LUCKSlinger... você possui um bracelete com jóias que podem ser coletadas de inimigos mortos ou encontradas no cenário... cada um dos pontos no bracelete pode ser ativado para garantir um campo de proteção, regarregamento de 'balas certeiras', para salvar Luckslinger de uma queda mortal ou ajudar o pato a localizar algo útil no cenário. O jogo também poderá promover má ou boa sorte, má sorte indicada com um breve aviso em cor vermelha e boa sorte com um breve aviso em cor dourada; a depender da situação um águia pode jogar pela janela coração de vida ou uma cascavel....

Problemas? Apenas um: Versão Linux reconhece o controle (Xpad) de uma forma diferente... o botão de rolar, que serve também para desviar de balas e é super necessário contra chefões, está trocado. Para rolar na versão Linux você coloca o stick direito para baixo. Também há uma repetição para o botão de start que é colocada no click do stick esquerdo, mas isso não realmente atrapalha muito.

E isso é o básico que se pode dizer de Luckslinger: simples, divertido e carismático jogo que junta conceitos clássicos em uma abordagem moderna e bem humorada. E vale bem os R$ 19,99 que pede.

This game is a perfect example of why Steam reviews need a "Kinda Recommended" button instead of yes or no, because Luckslinger has a lot of good, that is sadly bogged down by some questionable design choices and insipid difficulty. 
* Presentation
The game looks fairly average at best. The low-detail pixel art is ugly at times, but the use of colour and the emotions presented in animations give the game life. The different locations are all visually unique and sport some cool design choices, and each one has great atmosphere. The music is also really damn good, with some excellent hip-hop choices that really compliment the atmosphere. Overall the game has a great sense of charm with little details, like how people speak in record-vinyl scratching, or the clickclickclick of reloading your pistol. The story of the game is also really good, with some great dialouge that gives life to the characters- special note given to the main 6 bad guys of the game, who each have some interesting reasons for doing what they do.
* Gameplay
The game has a number of great ideas. It is a run and gun shooter with emphasis placed on Luck above all things- Luck is in fact a collectable, and can be used to turn bullets away from you, drop rewards and so on. This works in reverse too- low luck means bad things happen, and this puts an interesting spin on things. The game has a number of little details that make it fun, like a duck assist character,  a 6 shot ammo limit for your gun, and a throwing knife. The controls, however, make what could be an interesting take on a run and gun extremely frustrating. The Luckslinger frankly controls like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥. His jump arc is really impercise, his dodge roll is useful for exclusively bullets (meaning everything else must be dodged over) and has a cooldown, meaning it's useless to use in a firefight with a lot of people, which the game throws at you with alarm.  The game style, however, is simply not built for this kind of hectic firefight, so you end up dying a lot. Add the fact that your invincibility frames are non-existent to very small and you get a game trying to be a bullet hell that cannot handle being one. Oh, and he also cancels reloading by jumping or rolling, which makes reloading (which the game will NOT auto do for you) a huge pain in the ass, and more of a detriment than a factor of the game you need to work around, like Carry Capacity in Dark Souls. It's extremely frustrating to play this game because underneath the terrible controls is a genuinely intelligent spin on the run and gun genre, and to see such amateur failures bog it down is disheartening.
* Design
And here is where the game really ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed. Luckslinger is too hard for it's own good- in an attempt to be "oh so #Oldschool" Duckbridge made a game that is hard for the wrong reasons, including the aforementioned flaws in the gameplay section, but this extends into design. For starters, the basic difficulty mode is extremely cruel- there are checkpoints, but lose all your lives and you're back to the start. In any game like Castlevania, this is fine- most stages in that game are like 10 minutes long. In here, the stages easily surpass 20 minutes, which can make backtracking through the whooooolllleeee damn stage a huge pain in the ass, and not fun at all. Losing luck after every hit is also extremely annoying, as it causes a cycle of hurting every time you get hit, meaning you'll just keep losing. The game's level design leaves a lot to be desired, as instead of coming up with unique scenarios for you to fight through, it just swamps you with foes and says "deal with it". For a game that obviously wants to be played fast and risky, it sure is easy and reliable to cheese. These design and gameplay problems come together to for a game that tries to be hard and forgets to be fair- in a hard game like Super Meat Boy, every death is my fault and I know it, because the controls are so tight and the design is so fair that I never got frustrated at the game. Here, Luckslinger just made me want to put down the game and never play it again because I always felt my deaths were not preventable, which is a shame because the game does have some replay value and some great uses of player choice.

Overall, Luckslinger could have been a must buy with some great ideas and pretty good excecution, but in it's current state, plagued with rookie mistakes, it simply lies as an okay game that should be examined as how to NOT do difficulty.

As a fan of sphagetti westerns I love this game. The art direction perfectly captures the sphagetti western, the music (an interesting mix of hip hop and Morricone) is fantatastic, there's plenty of references to the best of the sphagetti western genre, and perhaps most importantly the gameplay is interesting and fun. Gamplay-wise the biggest thing that sets this game apart is the luck meter, you generally get luck by killing enemies which will build up your luck meter, when your luck meter is low you will fall into traps, enemies will burst out of haybales, windmill blades will fall on you and other unlucky things, when your luck is high none of these will happen, your duck companion will find hearts for you, and enemy bullets will sometimes miss you, you can also use half of your luck meter to temporarily make an aura of luck around you, which largely helps in avoiding large amounts of incoming fire.

First impressions...

A very challenging sidescrolling platform shootemup in which you play as a 'Man with no Name' silent type. Graphics are reminiscent of C64 era and the difficulty is brutal. The controls are a little tricky to get used to ('D' just doesn't feel right for shooting) but the remapping menu is so offputting I gave up and learnt the defaults.

The game works on a 'luck' system. Enemies you kill drop luck points that can be used to avoid elemental hazards (missed that jump? if you have enough luck you'll land on a roast chicken (?) and survive). 

Perhaps my main complaint aside from the controls is the checkpoint system. You accrue luck during a level, the idea being that by the time you get to the area boss you have enough luck to mitigate the difficulty. The trouble is, if that boss then kills you, you go back to the most recent checkpoint with your luck points reset. Given the game likes to put checkpoints just before the boss, it means if a boss kills you, subsequent battles will have to be fought without any luck on your side. My advice is to memorise map layouts and enemy patterns and just try not to ever die.

+ Looks and sounds great (the soundtrack is very good, though can be a bit repetetive)
+ Challenging
+ Luck system is a unique mechanic
+ Lots of Easter Eggs for Western fans
+ Pet duck
- Clunky controls
- Platforming lacks pinpoint precision
- Checkpoints work against the player and the core mechanic

I'm going to keep playing as its a lot of fun. I am happy to recommend the game, but be prepared to tear your hair out!
